title: Working Interests
metaTitle: Working Interests: Costs and Risks | Utah Owners
metaDescription: A working interest carries drilling and operating costs alongside royalty upside. Here's how Utah working interests differ from royalty ownership, and what to weigh.
heroLead: A working interest is the one mineral-related position that turns you into something closer to a co-operator than a passive owner, and that distinction has real financial consequences.
intro: Everything else in this guide describes ownership positions where you receive income without bearing cost — mineral rights, royalty interests, NPRIs, and even ORRIs all sit on the cost-free side of the ledger. A working interest is different: it's the operating interest in a lease, and holding one means you're responsible for your proportionate share of drilling, completion, and ongoing operating costs, on top of being entitled to a share of revenue. In exchange for taking on that cost exposure, a working interest owner typically receives a larger percentage of production revenue than a royalty owner would on the same well.

We occasionally hear from Utah families who inherited a working interest, often from a relative who was directly involved in a small drilling venture or partnership decades ago, and are surprised to learn that the position comes with ongoing financial obligations rather than simply a bigger check. That surprise is exactly why this interest type deserves its own careful look before deciding what to do with it.

sections.heading: What cost exposure actually looks like
paragraphs: A working interest owner is billed their proportionate share of expenses through what's called a joint interest billing, or JIB, covering everything from the original drilling and completion cost to ongoing operating expenses like workovers, equipment repairs, and eventually plugging and abandonment when the well reaches the end of its life. These bills arrive whether or not the well is currently profitable, and an owner who doesn't pay a cash call can face penalties under the joint operating agreement, including having their interest go non-consent on future operations or, in some structures, being subject to a lien.

This cost exposure is the core reason working interests are considered a fundamentally different risk category from royalty ownership. A royalty owner's downside in a bad month is simply a small or zero check. A working interest owner's downside can include being billed for expenses that exceed the well's revenue in a given period, particularly during a major workover or a low commodity price stretch.

sections.heading: Why most family-held working interests get sold
paragraphs: For a family without operating expertise or the appetite to review and pay joint interest billings on an ongoing basis, a working interest is often more liability than asset, even when the underlying well is a solid producer. Unlike a royalty interest, it requires active management: reviewing JIBs for accuracy, responding to authorization-for-expenditure requests before major operations, and staying current on payments to avoid penalty provisions.

This is a large part of why we see more working interests sold than held once they pass to a generation not directly involved in oil and gas operations. Converting a cost-bearing operating position into a lump sum removes both the ongoing cash-call exposure and the administrative burden of tracking joint interest billings, in exchange for giving up the larger revenue share a working interest carries while it's producing well.

sections.heading: How working interests get valued and sold
paragraphs: Pricing a working interest requires more diligence than a royalty interest, because a buyer needs to understand both the revenue side and the full cost picture: current operating expenses, any outstanding authorizations for expenditure, plugging liability that may eventually attach to the interest, and the terms of the underlying joint operating agreement. We review all of that before making an offer, and we're upfront that a working interest sale process typically takes a bit longer than a straightforward royalty sale because of the additional documentation involved.

If you've inherited or otherwise ended up holding a Utah working interest and aren't sure what obligations currently attach to it, that uncertainty itself is worth resolving quickly, since unpaid joint interest billings can accumulate penalties the longer they go unaddressed. We can help identify the operator and pull your current standing as a first step, whether or not you ultimately decide to sell.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a working interest and a royalty interest?
faqs.answer: A royalty interest receives production revenue with no cost obligation. A working interest receives a larger revenue share but is also responsible for its proportionate share of drilling and operating costs, billed through joint interest billings.

faqs.question: Can I be billed for costs even if I don't want to pay?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, if you hold the working interest and don't formally elect non-consent on a specific operation under the joint operating agreement. Unpaid joint interest billings can trigger penalty provisions, so it's worth understanding your specific agreement's terms.

faqs.question: Why would someone sell a working interest instead of keeping the higher revenue share?
faqs.answer: The ongoing cost exposure and administrative burden of reviewing billings and expenditure requests often outweighs the benefit for a family without operating involvement, especially compared to the simplicity of a royalty interest. A sale converts that ongoing obligation into a clean, known amount.

faqs.question: Does a working interest carry plugging liability?
faqs.answer: It can, depending on the joint operating agreement and how the interest is structured. This is one of the reasons working interest valuations require more diligence than royalty interests, and it's something we review carefully before making an offer.
